I'd say start off small. A tomato plant and summer squash would be fairly easy and a good introduction. Perhaps a bush bean as well. This fall, you can plant a crop of onions and garlic and let them go dormant over the winter. When spring comes, they'll start growing again.

With tomatoes, be careful what variety you get. There's determinant that grows to a certain size, it's fruit ripens, then it dies. These are smaller and much more manageable. Think 4-5 feet. Then there's indeterminant tomatoes. These will keep growing indefinitely until something else kills them (winter/disease) or they're not able to produce enough nutrients to keep itself alive. I'm growing Cherokee Purple right now and it's already 6 feet tall and will most likely grow taller than the 8 foot cage I have around it.

As for summer squash, anything really. If you want to harvest seeds for next year, choose something that's not a hybrid. I'm currently growing Black Beauty Zucchini (50 days til maturity). You'll often see people grow both yellow squash and zucchini. Next year I'll likely try Desi Summer Squash, mainly because it's unique and it starts producing at 40 days instead of 50 days like most early varieties.

As for beans, go for a bush bean instead of a pole bean. A bush bean grows like a bush (surprise!). A pole bean grows up a trellis, fence, pole, etc. As you can see from the picture, I purchased Romano and Strike bush beans. If you want a more unique variety/coloring, check out this site.

Garlic/Onions: Just find some that'll be fine going dormant over the winter, particularly for your type of winters.
